newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban set tough terms for peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban set tough terms for peace talks.

text.p: A leader of Afghanistan's Taleban militia said on Saturday opposition groups must accept it as the country's government as a condition for peace talks and a ceasefire.

"We are not against peace, and the opposition should accept the rule of the Islamic State of Afghanistan for there to be any kind of talks or ceasefire and (accept) that the restoration of tranquility be based on Islamic principles," Mullah Mohammad Rabbani told reporters.

Rabbani, head of the Taleban interim council in Kabul, was referring to what the militia calls a caretaker government that would give way to a government formed of all Afghanistan's warring factions after peace talks.

No country has formally recognised the Taleban government and frequent attempts by the United Nations, Pakistan and now Iran have so far failed to bring reconciliation between the Taleban and the government they drove from Kabul last September.
Leaders of the former government were in Tehran on Saturday for peace talks hosted by the Iranian government, but no Taleban delegation was present.
Rabbani said this was because the Iranian invitation to attend did not arrive in time.
"These talks will not have any result and nobody from Taleban has gone to Tehran because the invitation came late yesterday," he said.
Relations between mainly Shi'ite Iran and the mostly ethnic Pashtun Sunni Moslem Taleban, who control most of a country devastated by 18 years of war, have been strained.
Tehran recognises the ousted government of Burhanuddin Rabbani -- no relation to Mullah Rabbani.

The Taleban are fighting forces of the deposed government's ethnic Tajik military chief Ahmad Shah Massoud and his ally, Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, 110 km (70 miles) north of Kabul near the Hindu Kush mountains, where the population is mostly Tajik.
Thousands of people fled the area as the Taleban moved back in over the past few days, some saying they had been told to leave by the black-turbanned Taleban fighters.
However, Rabbani said allegations of ethnic cleansing were enemy propaganda.
"It is all baseless that we are forcing the locals to vacate these areas. We know the ones who rose against us. Their number is very limited and we have told them to leave temporarily," he said.
The Taleban have made rapid advances in the area over the past few days, taking back ground they first won and then lost again in the weeks after they took Kabul.
They were driven back in part by a rash of attacks by villagers behind their lines. Taleban commanders say they will not make the same mistake again and are searching all houses for weapons.
